description: Palmyra was an ancient desert city whose caravans relied on astronomy, and its trade routes drew scholars and star-watchers from across the world. Palmyra Ensemble develops DUST-GUARD, a concept that keeps Mars rover camera windows clear of dust using a PTFE coating, an electrodynamic dust shield, and image restoration. Our 2026 paper tests whether this design can work, separating proven results from estimates that still need laboratory validation.
summary:
DUST-GUARD is our idea for keeping Mars rover cameras clear. Dust that settles on a camera window makes the photos blurry, and blurry photos are less useful to the scientists waiting for them back on Earth. Our concept has three parts: a PTFE coating that might let dust slide off more easily, a thin electrodynamic shield that pushes particles away from the glass, and image processing to clean up what’s left.

Our 2026 paper asks whether this can actually work. The shield is the part with the strongest support so far. Earlier NASA and academic tests showed it removing most of the dust in low-pressure carbon dioxide, the kind of air found on Mars, and it needs very little power. The coating is less certain. It would only help if dust particles sit noticeably farther from the coated glass than from bare glass, and we don’t yet know its effect on how much light gets through or how long it lasts. Image processing helps with haze in the air, but it can’t bring back a view that dust has completely blocked.

We put our honest odds at roughly 57% for the shield working as intended, 20 to 25% for the coating giving a measurable benefit, and 10 to 15% for the full system working in a first round of testing. Those numbers are estimates, not measurements, and the next step is a controlled lab test to find out which way they go.
details:
DUST-GUARD: Keeping Mars Rover Cameras Clear

The challenge
Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars

The problem we picked
A landscape only becomes science if the camera can see it. Every rover photo has to pass through a small window first, and dust on that window means light never arrives. Dust piles up on exposed rover hardware over time, as these views show.


Opportunity (top) and Curiosity (bottom), earlier views on the left and dustier ones on the right. This is dust on solar arrays and the rover deck, not a camera window, but cameras sit outside in the same air.

Dust in the air is a separate problem, and we try to keep the two apart.


Opportunity’s view as atmospheric dust thickened in 2007, with optical depth rising from 0.94 to 4.7. A clean window can’t fix this. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Cornell, PIA09935.


Opportunity’s last transmitted image, during the June 2018 dust storm. The black band is missing data and the speckle is camera noise. It shows what losing a view looks like, not dust on a lens. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Cornell/ASU, PIA22929.

Dimming isn’t the whole story. Uniform dimming alone doesn’t lower contrast, but scattered light does, and that’s what washes out fine detail.


Our analytical illustrations: direct light falls off exponentially with optical depth, and contrast drops once scattered light is added. These curves are illustrative, not measured rover data.

What we did
We didn’t build hardware. We worked through the physics of a three-part window: a PTFE coating to make dust less sticky, an electrodynamic shield that pushes particles off the glass, and image processing for whatever is left. We took published NASA and university results, checked what each one really proves, and ran the numbers ourselves. Some of the coated-shield data came from lunar dust studies, which is a useful link back to the challenge. Where no measurement exists, we used assumptions and labeled them as such.

What we found
The electrodynamic shield has the strongest evidence. Published tests removed 90 to 95 percent of dust in low-pressure CO₂, and the screen needs only about 0.3 to 0.9 joules a day. The coating is the shaky part. By our math it only helps if dust sits about 1.45 times farther from it than from bare glass, and nobody has measured that yet. We also found a break-even point: the coating pays off when the window is badly fouled and costs you when it’s only lightly dusty.


Left, our estimated chance that each idea passes a lab test. Right, when the coating helps and when a bare shielded window does better. The estimates are our own judgment, and the right-hand curves use assumed values.

How sure are we?
About 57 percent for the shield on its own, 20 to 25 percent for a measurable benefit from the coating, and 10 to 15 percent for the whole system working in a first round of testing. They’re modest on purpose. We’d rather show the weak points than claim a result we haven’t earned.

What comes next
A controlled lab test using dust from an analog site: a bare window and a coated one, shield on and off, with and without dust, all measured for how much light gets through. That would replace our assumptions with real numbers.
